questions.question: Q: Why is evaluation important in citizenship action?

points.text: Evaluation is important because it assesses whether the action achieved its aims, identifies what worked and what didn't, provides evidence of impact, and helps improve future actions. In the AQA exam, evaluation is worth the most marks (up to 24 marks on Paper 2 Section B).

questions.question: Q: What is the difference between quantitative and qualitative evidence in evaluation?

points.text: Quantitative evidence is numerical — e.g. 250 signatures collected, 80% of students supported the campaign. Qualitative evidence is descriptive — e.g. quotes from stakeholders about changing attitudes, observations about increased awareness, testimonials from participants.

questions.question: Q: How should you structure an evaluation of your citizenship action?

points.text: Restate your original aims, assess whether each aim was met using evidence, discuss which methods worked well and why, identify what didn't work and analyse reasons, explain what you would do differently, and reflect on what you learned about citizenship and democracy.

markScheme.exemplarAnswer: My citizenship action aimed to improve recycling facilities in my school, where a survey showed 78% of students wanted better options. My research included surveying 150 students, interviewing the site manager, and reviewing the school's current recycling provision. My strategy was to combine a petition with a presentation to the school council and a social media campaign. I chose these methods because they involved different stakeholders and created multiple routes to influence the headteacher. The petition collected 210 signatures in two weeks, exceeding my target of 150. The social media campaign reached 500 views on Instagram but engagement was low — only 30 likes and 5 shares. This showed that while awareness was raised, it did not translate into active support. Presenting to the school council was effective — they voted to support the proposal, giving it legitimacy. The headteacher agreed to fund three new recycling bins and a poster campaign, partially meeting my aim. However, my action had limitations. I focused on bins but did not address the lack of education about what can be recycled. I struggled to maintain momentum after the launch. With hindsight, I would have involved the eco-club from the start. The impact was measurable — recycling rates increased by 25% in the first month.
